A utilitarian should oppose this motion, because blame is justified by its effects, and blaming careful people in proportion to harm produces worse effects than the alternatives. Blame, punishment and praise are practices, and practices are justified by their consequences. Their job is to make people more careful in future. Blaming a team that did everything right teaches the industry that care does not protect you, which weakens the incentive to take care at all.

If blame scaled with harm regardless of care, the rational response for builders would be to avoid high-stakes uses altogether. That would withdraw useful systems from medicine and transport, where the expected benefits are large, and make people worse off overall. If an audited diagnostic model makes one fatal error in a million cases, blaming its builders fully might stop the next team building a model that saves thousands.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that treating blame as a pure incentive misses that a good person acknowledges harm they caused, and a culture that only manages incentives breeds builders who shrug. Acknowledging harm can itself be encouraged, and it should be, because it helps victims and keeps builders attentive. But acknowledgement is not proportional blame, and confusing the two would make the practice worse at preventing the next harm. Aim blame where it can change what happens next, and the careful builder is the wrong target.

The motion gets blame backwards. We should blame in whatever way best prevents future harm, and that means rewarding care, not punishing it when luck runs out. What should be blamed is what could have been done better: skipped tests, ignored warnings, rushed releases. Tracking those failures directly gives builders a clear reason to avoid them, while blame by outcome gives them a lottery.

If blame scaled with harm regardless of care, the rational response for builders would be to avoid high-stakes uses altogether. That would withdraw useful systems from medicine and transport, where the expected benefits are large, and make people worse off overall. A pilot who followed every procedure in a freak storm is not grounded for life, because that would teach other pilots nothing useful.

The useful question is which incentives reduce future harm, and blaming bad luck is not one of them.

Blame is a tool for changing future behaviour, so it should track what would have prevented the harm, and punishing care that failed by chance prevents nothing. There are better tools for the harm itself. Compensation schemes and insurance can make victims whole without pretending the builders were at fault. Separating compensation from blame lets us help the injured and keep the incentives right at the same time.

Tracking those failures directly gives builders a clear reason to avoid them, while blame by outcome gives them a lottery. Vaccine makers are shielded by compensation schemes because blaming them for rare reactions would make vaccines scarcer, and far more people would die.

A Stoic will object that blame belongs to faulty judgement and nothing else, so its usefulness is irrelevant: a careful builder is blameless whether or not blaming her would deter anyone. In ordinary cases the two views agree, since faulty judgement is what we want to deter. Where they come apart, the question is what the practice of blame is for, and a practice that helps nobody has no claim on us. Blame laid on people who could not have acted otherwise is suffering added to the world with nothing prevented in return.

Nobody can predict everything an AI will do. It would be unfair to blame engineers for things they could not have known, so they should not be blamed at all if they followed the rules.
